blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Raw data are data exactly as recorded: an unsorted, unsummarised list of observations. Organising raw data means sorting them and counting how many fall at each value or in each range, usually as a frequency distribution (§1.4.1).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Here are the weights (kg) of the 30 children seen at the under-five clinic today, in the order they walked in:

11.2, 9.8, 14.1, 10.0, 12.3, 13.6, 11.1, 11.9, 12.6, 9.4, 13.8, 15.3, 13.4, 12.9, 9.1, 9.7, 11.6, 10.3, 11.5, 8.6, 14.8, 10.5, 11.0, 12.4, 11.8, 10.8, 12.0, 13.1, 11.4, 14.4.

Their mean is 11.8 kg, but the list itself is hard to read. Sorting it and counting how many fall in each range is the first step towards seeing its shape.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Sorted, the same 30 weights run from 8.6 kg to 15.3 kg. Counting them into 2-kg ranges (§1.4.1) turns a wall of 30 numbers into a four-row table.

points.html: Raw data = data as collected, with no summarising applied.

Many statistics (the mean, the median) can be computed straight from the raw list; a frequency table is a convenient precursor, and it is required only for grouped-data formulas and for charts such as the histogram (§4.3).

blocks.html: Frequency Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A frequency distribution is a table of values (or ranges of values, called class intervals) alongside the number of observations, the frequency, in each.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Instead of listing 30 weights, count how many fall in each 2-kg class. Patterns invisible in the raw list, such as where most values cluster, become visible at a glance.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Weight (kg) Frequency
8 to <10 5
10 to <12 12
12 to <14 9
14 to <16 4
Total 30

Each class includes its lower end and excludes its upper end, so the child weighing exactly 10.0 kg is counted in “10 to <12”, and the child weighing 12.0 kg in “12 to <14”. Most children today weighed between 10 and 14 kg.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
How many classes? Sturges (1926) started from an ideal distribution of N = 2ᵏ⁻¹ items spread over k classes in proportion to the numbers in a row of Pascal’s triangle (the binomial coefficients, §5.7.1.2): 1; 1, 1; 1, 2, 1; 1, 3, 3, 1; 1, 4, 6, 4, 1; …, each number the sum of the two above it (for 16 items and 5 classes: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1). Each number feeds two numbers in the row below, so each row adds up to twice the row above: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. The row with k numbers therefore adds up to 2ᵏ⁻¹, so

N = 2ᵏ⁻¹ ⟹ k − 1 = log₂N ⟹ k = 1 + log₂N = 1 + log₁₀N ÷ log₁₀2 = 1 + 3.322 log₁₀N

where ⟹ reads “which gives”. The class width is roughly the range divided by k.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. log₁₀30 = 1.477.
  2. 3.322 × 1.477 = 4.907.
  3. k = 1 + 4.907 = 5.91, so Sturges suggests about 6 classes.
  4. Range = 15.3 − 8.6 = 6.7 kg; width = 6.7 ÷ 5.91 = 1.13 kg.

Result: Sturges’ rule suggests 6 classes of about 1.1 kg; the table above uses 4 classes of 2 kg. Both are defensible. With only 30 children, 6 classes would leave several classes with 1–3 children each, and 1.13-kg limits are awkward to read; 2-kg classes with whole-number limits are easier to read and compare with other clinics. Sturges’ rule is a starting point, not a requirement.

points.html: Two forms exist: ungrouped (a frequency for each distinct value) and grouped (a frequency for each class interval); see §1.4.2.

Classes must be mutually exclusive (no value fits two classes) and exhaustive (every value fits one). Equal widths are the usual convention and make a histogram easy to read; unequal classes, such as the WHO anaemia bands of §1.4.2, are legitimate when a clinical classification demands them, but a histogram must then plot frequency density (§4.3.1).
Sturges’ rule, k = 1 + 3.322 log₁₀N (Sturges, 1926), is a convention; it assumes a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped spread, and readability or a clinical classification may justify a different k.
A frequency distribution is the input for the histogram (§4.3) and for grouped-data formulas for the mean, median and mode (Chapter 2).

blocks.html: Grouped vs Ungrouped Data

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Ungrouped data list every distinct value with its own frequency. Grouped data put ranges of values into class intervals and report the frequency per interval, giving up some detail for a readable table. Each class interval has class limits (the smallest and largest values that can be recorded in it) and class boundaries (the points on the continuous scale that separate adjacent classes, halfway between one class’s upper limit and the next class’s lower limit).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
If a variable takes a handful of values, such as number of ANC visits (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 …), list each value: that is ungrouped. If it is continuous or has many distinct values, such as weight to 0.1 kg across 500 children, bucket the values into ranges: that is grouped.

Limits and boundaries differ because measurements are rounded. Haemoglobin recorded to 0.1 g/dL might be grouped as 7.0–9.9 and 10.0–10.9: those are class limits. A true value of 9.96 g/dL is recorded as 10.0, so the real dividing line between the two classes is 9.95: that is the class boundary. The class 7.0–9.9 has boundaries 6.95 and 9.95, width 3.0, and class mark (mid-point) (6.95 + 9.95) ÷ 2 = 8.45 g/dL.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Ungrouped: number of diarrhoeal episodes in the past month among the 100 children of the clinic register: 0 episodes, 41 children; 1, 35; 2, 16; 3, 5; 4, 3.

Grouped: haemoglobin grouped into WHO’s severity bands for children aged 24–59 months: severe <7.0 g/dL, moderate 7.0–9.9, mild 10.0–10.9, no anaemia ≥11.0 (WHO, 2024). Here grouping mirrors a clinical classification. The bands depend on the population: WHO’s 2024 guideline gives different cut-offs for children 6–23 months (anaemia below 10.5 g/dL), for non-pregnant women (below 12.0) and for men (below 13.0), and by trimester in pregnancy. Always state the population when you quote a cut-off.

points.html: Choose grouped or ungrouped by how many distinct values the variable takes, not by whether it is qualitative or quantitative.
Grouping loses information: from the table alone you know a reading lies in 7.0–9.9, not its exact value.
Grouped-data calculations use the class mark as a stand-in for every value in the class; the approximation is better when classes are narrow.
Write classes so that no value is ambiguous: either “8 to <10” (half-open) or limits that do not overlap (“8.0–9.9, 10.0–11.9”). A table reading “8–10, 10–12” leaves 10.0 with two homes.

Strictly, a weight recorded as 10.0 kg stands for anything from 9.95 to 10.05 kg, so the true boundaries of “10 to <12” in recorded values are 9.95 and 11.95. This book’s grouped calculations ignore that 0.05-kg shift and use the mid-points 9, 11, 13 and 15 kg.

blocks.html: Relative and Cumulative Frequency

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Relative frequency is a class’s frequency divided by the total number of observations. Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies up to and including a class.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: “What fraction of the children are in this class?” is relative frequency. “How many are in this class or below?” is cumulative frequency. Relative frequency lets you compare a sample of 30 with a sample of 3,000; cumulative frequency is the basis of percentiles and the ogive (§4.3.3, a cumulative frequency curve).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Weight (kg) f Relative f (%) Cumulative f Cumulative relative f (%)
8 to <10 5 16.7 5 16.7
10 to <12 12 40.0 17 56.7
12 to <14 9 30.0 26 86.7
14 to <16 4 13.3 30 100.0

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Relative frequency of 10 to <12 kg = 12 ÷ 30 = 0.40 = 40%.
  2. Cumulative frequency up to and including 10 to <12 kg = 5 + 12 = 17.
  3. Cumulative relative frequency = 17 ÷ 30 = 56.7%.

Result: 17 of the 30 children (56.7%) weigh under 12 kg.

points.html: Relative frequencies sum to 1 (100%), apart from rounding.
The last cumulative frequency equals N.
Read cumulative frequency at a class boundary: “17 children weigh under 12 kg”, not “12 kg or less”.
Cumulative relative frequency is the basis for the grouped median, quartiles and percentiles (§2.3, §3.4) and for the ogive.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 1.4

questions.prompt: List, in order, the steps that turn a raw, unsorted list of 200 haemoglobin readings into something you could read a percentile from.
questions.answer: 1. Start from the raw list. (2) Sort it and choose class intervals with unambiguous limits (e.g. 7.0–7.9, 8.0–8.9 … or half-open classes). (3) Count the frequency in each class (grouped, because 200 readings to 0.1 g/dL have many distinct values). (4) Add relative frequency and cumulative frequency (and cumulative relative frequency). (5) Read or interpolate the percentile from the cumulative relative frequency column, using class boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why group haemoglobin readings but not “number of children per household”?
questions.answer: Haemoglobin is continuous with many distinct decimal values; listing each would give a table almost as long as the data. Number of children per household takes a few small whole numbers (0, 1, 2, 3 …), so an ungrouped table stays short and loses nothing.

questions.prompt: Using the diarrhoea table in §1.4.2 (0: 41, 1: 35, 2: 16, 3: 5, 4: 3), compute the cumulative frequency up to 1 episode and the percentage of children with 2 or more episodes.
questions.answer:
1. Cumulative frequency up to 1 episode = 41 + 35 = 76 children.
  2. Children with 2 or more = 16 + 5 + 3 = 24 (equivalently 100 − 76 = 24).
  3. Percentage = 24 ÷ 100 = 24%.

blocks.html: Sources of Health Data in India

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A source of health data is a system that routinely or periodically records health-related events or characteristics for a defined population. Sources differ in what they count, which population forms the denominator (the group the count is divided by to make a rate or proportion), how often they report, and how their data can go wrong. Data quality is judged on dimensions that include completeness (did every unit that should report, report?), timeliness (did reports arrive by the deadline?), internal consistency (do the numbers agree with each other and over time?) and external comparison (do they agree with other sources, such as surveys?) (WHO, 2020). Validity, whether a recorded value measures what it claims to (Chapter 16), sits underneath all four.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Most numbers a Community Medicine resident quotes come from secondary data (§1.2), so you must know each source’s denominator and blind spots. A useful split: counting systems try to record every event (census, civil registration, surveillance); sample surveys measure a probability sample (units chosen by a random mechanism, Chapter 6) and estimate the rest (SRS, NFHS); facility systems record people who reached a facility (HMIS, hospital registries). Counting systems fail through under-registration; surveys through sampling error (chance differences between sample and population, §6.4) and non-response; facility systems through the people who never came.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Source What it measures Unit and denominator How often Known weakness
Census of India Population size and composition, down to village level Every household; the denominator for most rates Decennial; 2011 is the latest census with published tables Denominators for later years must be projected, and projections drift as years pass from the census
Civil Registration System (CRS) Births, deaths, stillbirths; compulsory under the Registration of Births and Deaths (RBD) Act, 1969 Every registered event, at the place of occurrence Continuous; annual report Completeness and promptness vary by state
Sample Registration System (SRS) Birth rate, death rate, infant mortality rate (IMR), other fertility and mortality indicators Continuous enumeration plus a six-monthly independent survey in sample villages and urban blocks Annual estimates Sample-based: sampling error; estimates are for the nation, states and natural divisions, not districts
Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) Medically certified cause of death, coded by the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) Certified deaths only Annual report Only 22.3% of registered deaths were certified in 2022
National Family Health Survey (NFHS) Fertility, child health, nutrition, anaemia, blood pressure and blood glucose Probability sample of households, women 15–49, men 15–54 Periodic (NFHS-5 fieldwork June 2019–April 2021) Survey design must be used in analysis (§15.2.6)
Health Management Information System (HMIS) Service delivery (ANC, deliveries, immunisation) reported by facilities Service users at reporting facilities Monthly, web-based portal since 2008 Denominator is service users, not the population; reporting by private facilities has needed specific effort to improve
Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP / IHIP) Epidemic-prone diseases: Syndromic (S), Presumptive (P) and Laboratory (L) forms Auxiliary nurse-midwives (ANMs) at sub-centres (S), medical officers (P), laboratories (L) Continuous, case-based entry on the IHIP portal Captures only people who reach a sub-centre, facility or laboratory
National Cancer Registry Programme (NCRP) Cancer incidence, mortality and patterns Population-based registries (PBCRs: defined area) and hospital-based registries (HBCRs: patients of one hospital) Periodic reports Registry areas cover part of the country; HBCRs describe patients, not populations

Sources: Census of India; Office of the Registrar General, India (ORGI) (2022, CRS report; 2022, MCCD report; 2020, SRS Statistical Report); Data for India (2025, CRS and SRS); DHS Program (NFHS-5, India’s Demographic and Health Survey); Meghani et al. (2022, HMIS); Singh et al. (2023, IDSP-IHIP); ICMR-NCDIR (2020).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
A block has 40 sub-centres expected to send their monthly HMIS report. By the deadline 29 reports have arrived; 5 more arrive late; 6 never arrive.

  1. Reports received = 29 + 5 = 34. Completeness = 34 ÷ 40 = 85.0%.
  2. On-time reports = 29. As a share of expected reports: 29 ÷ 40 = 72.5%. As a share of reports received: 29 ÷ 34 = 85.3%.
  3. State which denominator you used; tools differ, and the two figures answer different questions.

Result: completeness 85.0%, timeliness 72.5% of expected reports. Any block total built on these reports undercounts services by whatever the 6 missing sub-centres delivered.

A second calculation shows why a denominator matters. In 2022, CRS recorded 86,49,930 deaths, and 22.3% of them were medically certified: 0.223 × 86,49,930 ≈ 19.3 lakh deaths with a certified cause. Cause-of-death proportions from MCCD describe those 19.3 lakh deaths, not the remaining 77.7% of registered deaths or any unregistered ones.

points.html: Ask of every source: who is counted, who is the denominator, how often, and who is missed.
CRS aims to count every event (ORGI, 2022); SRS samples to give reliable annual estimates of birth rate, death rate and IMR (ORGI, 2020). Rates from the two can differ.
HMIS and IDSP counts are facility-based: a rise can mean more disease, more care-seeking, or better reporting. Check completeness before reading a trend.
NFHS is a complex survey (strata, clusters, weights); unweighted analysis of its data can be biased (§15.2.6).
Registries: a PBCR can give incidence rates for its area; an HBCR cannot, because it has no population denominator.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 1.5

questions.prompt: Why can a hospital-based cancer registry describe the pattern of cancers among its patients but not the incidence of cancer in the district?
questions.answer: Incidence needs new cases divided by the population they arose from. An HBCR records the patients who came to that hospital, from an undefined catchment and filtered by referral, distance and cost; it has no population denominator. It can say what share of its patients have each cancer site. A population-based registry, which tries to record every new case in a defined area with a census-based population, can give incidence rates.

questions.prompt: A district’s IDSP data show acute diarrhoeal disease cases doubling this month. Give three explanations other than a true doubling of disease.
questions.answer: 1. Better reporting: more sub-centres or facilities reported this month (completeness rose), or a new private facility started reporting. (2) More care-seeking: a campaign, a new facility or free ORS distribution brought more people to health workers. (3) Artefacts: late reports from last month entered this month, duplicate entries, or a change in case definition or form. Check completeness and timeliness before reading the trend.

questions.prompt: In a month, 50 primary health centres (PHCs) should report; 44 reports arrive, 36 of them by the deadline. Compute completeness and timeliness (as a share of expected reports).
questions.answer:
1. Completeness = 44 ÷ 50 = 88%.
  2. Timeliness = 36 ÷ 50 = 72% of expected reports (36 ÷ 44 = 81.8% of reports received).
